subject: AI & Agents
title: ELIZA: The First Chatbot
description: A 60-second lesson on ELIZA: The First Chatbot.

hook.text: In 1966, people poured out their feelings to a computer program. They knew it wasn't real. They didn't care.

buildup.text: Joseph Weizenbaum built ELIZA at MIT. It mimicked a therapist using simple pattern matching.

discovery.text: ELIZA matched keywords and rephrased your input as questions. 'I'm sad' became 'Why are you sad?'

twist.text: Weizenbaum was horrified that people formed emotional bonds with something so simple.

climax.text: He wrote a book warning that humans anthropomorphize machines too easily.

punchline.text: The first chatbot taught us more about humans than machines.

quiz.question: What technique did ELIZA use to simulate conversation?
options: Simple pattern matching and keyword rephrasing

details.summary: ELIZA, created in 1966 by Joseph Weizenbaum, simulated a psychotherapist by matching keywords and reflecting statements back. Users formed emotional bonds with it despite its extremely simple rules.
details.whyItMatters: ELIZA revealed that humans anthropomorphize machines with minimal prompting. This insight remains relevant today as millions form attachments to far more sophisticated chatbots.
takeaways: ELIZA used simple pattern matching to simulate conversation
Users formed emotional connections despite knowing it was a program
The ELIZA effect describes human tendency to anthropomorphize AI

faq.question: How did ELIZA actually work?
faq.answer: ELIZA matched keywords in user input and applied transformation rules. If you said 'I am sad,' it might respond 'Why are you sad?' It had no understanding — just pattern matching and rephrasing.

faq.question: Why is the ELIZA effect important today?
faq.answer: Modern chatbots are vastly more sophisticated, making the tendency to attribute emotions and intelligence to AI even stronger. The ELIZA effect warns us to maintain awareness that chat AI does not truly understand.
